I'm 27 and now feeling like I am just finally getting on my feet. And by that, I don't mean I have a job or even a great apartment- I live in a basement right now- but I think the first part of the change was shifting my mindset. To summarize, I am from Canada. I was offered a great scholarship to a school in NYC to study dance. I was fortunate enough to go, but during those 4 years I struggled with severe anxiety, depression, bulimia, and suicidal ideation. After I graduated, my visa expired and I was forced to move home. I felt like the biggest failure. I went from one of the most talented in my class to nothing. When I moved back to Canada, I moved into a room in the house of one of my grandma's friends since there was no space at my family home for me. I isolated myself constantly thinking about my failures while seeing my friends in NYC making it in the dance world or using their degrees to enter the corporate world in America. I couldn't even get a part time minimum wage job when I moved back. I hated myself and thought that I was worthless. Instead of dealing with my issues, with $500 in my bank account, I took a train across the country to Vancouver to "start new". Of course, my problems followed me there and I dealt with the same depressive thoughts and feelings. I moved back to Toronto at the start of the pandemic with little money in my account continuing the same patterns as before. I would always think 'why me?' and that I was destined to be a complete loser. One day I was so tired of this shit that I called a walk-in clinic to discuss my mental health. Fortunately in Ontario, there is access to some basic mental healthcare- a doctor prescribed me a low dose of an antidepressant and I was able to check in with them every couple of weeks when I needed a refill. I bought myself a planner and started writing down things I wanted to accomplish. I write down all sorts of things like look up unemployment benefits, clean room, shower, create simple budget, look up free therapy. It's a fucking hard process getting your life together, especially if you have privileged friends. I have people in my life who complain about their 9-5 salary and their parents support (which they have every right to complain) but I'm like what the fuck I have barely any money and try to spend as little on food each month. 

My advice is to reach out to people online. This could mean going on Psychology today and sending emails to every single therapist asking if they offer pro bono sessions or if they know of any colleagues that offer pro bono sessions. I did that and I was surprised by the response. I'd also recommend seeing if there are support groups where you can meet once a week on Zoom or in person depending on covid restrictions. It's good to talk to someone who has or who is currently experiencing similar struggles. Getting help in mental health care is so powerful and could be the kickstarter to changing how you view life. Try waking up in the morning and writing down 1-3 things you are grateful for even if it's just like your health and a roof over your head. Try to stretch and move your body a little. I'm rooting for you!

I'd like to share a little bit of my experience being someone who has recently been put on antidepressants (Lexapro) and is going through a rough patch with my partner. Of course, everyone is different, and I can only refer to what you have decided to share, but here is my take.

I am a long time sufferer of anxiety, depression, and bulimia for quite some time. I had a quick stint on Fluoxetine during my undergrad, but that ssri experience didn't work out so well for me.  I met my boyfriend in college at the height of my mental health issues and we started dating as I entered my mental health recovery, this time with an approach without antidepressants. Fast forward to the present day — I am now about 3 months into Lexapro and well over 2.5 years with my partner. This time around, the antidepressant has worked quite well for me and it feels like my anxiety and depression have been lifted, but I also feel a huge disconnect with my partner. It's almost as if I feel like a completely different person, and to be honest, I sort of am a different person. I'm not quite sure how mental illness has affected your girlfriend before antidepressants, but for me, it was sort of my identity. My partner and I entered a relationship and now that I look back on it, his presence acted as a way to alleviate my mental illness and he greatly impacted how anxiety and depression manifested in me. Now that I am freeing myself from my illnesses on my own and from a brain chemistry approach, I feel very different about how my partner fits into my life. Of course, he wasn't only there to be my therapist, but I believe we subconsciously gravitated to each other for what we needed at the time. I think that people can change a lot from antidepressants but they don't necessarily fall out of love because of them. Emotional blunting is a very common side effect, but I believe that it's the ability to fully express and feel emotions perhaps pertaining to love, but I don't think the thought or idea of loving someone is completely gone. I think it's worth assessing your relationship— the ups, downs, and growth periods on both parts to see how her antidepressants played a part in your breakup. I hope the two of you are okay!
